Hard times

Divorce and separation

Separating is one of the most stressful life changes. How it usually unfolds, what affects children and what helps you rebuild.

On Holmes and Rahe's scale, divorce ranked second among the most stressful events, behind only the death of a spouse. That is no surprise: a separation changes at once a person's love life, home, finances, relationship with their children and often their circle of friends.

How it usually unfolds

Studies that follow people for years show that distress peaks in the months around the separation and that most people return to their usual level of wellbeing within one or two years. There are important differences: for those in a highly conflictual relationship, separating is often a relief, while those who did not expect or want it find it harder. A minority develop depression, problem drinking or other difficulties that need help.

Children

What harms children most is not the separation itself but the conflict between parents, especially when children are caught in the middle: carrying messages, hearing criticism of the other parent or feeling they have to choose. The psychologist Mavis Hetherington followed hundreds of families for decades and found that 75 to 80% of children of divorced parents became well-adjusted adults. It helps to explain the decision together, in words suited to their age, to make clear it is not their fault, to keep routines and to let them love both parents.

What tends to help

  • Allowing yourself to grieve. Even if the decision is yours, a life plan is lost, and it is normal to feel sadness, anger and guilt.
  • Writing, with care. In a study by David Sbarra of recently separated people, writing about the emotions of the separation did not help everyone: those who tended to ruminate did worse than with neutral writing. Writing can help if it puts experience in order; if it only feeds rumination, it is better to stop.
  • Looking after social support. Friends and family are the main buffer; avoid isolating yourself.
  • Using family mediation for arrangements about children and property. It reduces conflict and tends to produce more lasting agreements than court cases.
  • Not rushing big decisions, such as moving far away or moving in with someone new, in the first months.

References

  1. Holmes, T. H. y Rahe, R. H. (1967). The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 11(2), 213–218.
  2. Amato, P. R. (2000). The consequences of divorce for adults and children. Journal of Marriage and Family, 62(4), 1269–1287.
  3. Hetherington, E. M. y Kelly, J. (2002). For Better or for Worse: Divorce Reconsidered. Nueva York: Norton.
  4. Sbarra, D. A. et al. (2013). Expressive writing can impede emotional recovery following marital separation. Clinical Psychological Science, 1(2), 120–134.
